segments.t: KITCO News onsite coverage of the New Orleans Investment Conference is presented by Dakota
Gold.
Hey everyone, welcome back to the New Orleans Investment Conference.
I'm Jeremy Safran.
Now, after its third quarter results, Big Tech lost nearly $900 billion in market value.
The bond market is moving like it knows something.
The 10-year Treasury yield is back below where it stood just the day before the Fed
hiked back in September.
Gold obviously sold off hard today on October 30, down more than $120 at one point and my
guest has made the same call three times this week.
If Tech keeps falling, the Fed doesn't hike in December.
He's also written what would mean for the dollar, of course, what it would mean for
gold.
Peter Boogvar is the Chief Investment Officer at One Point BFG Wealth Partners and the
editor of the book report.
Good to see you again Peter.
Good to see you Jeremy.
Thanks for having me.
Very interesting day.
I was talking about this before coming on camera.
Obviously these moves have been quick.
We're seeing the sell-off happen.
You've made the case three times this week.
Why does Tech get a vote at the Fed?
So a couple of things.
What's going on in Tech today is not just out of nowhere, there's been a progression
of events that sort of led us into this.
On the hardware side, particularly semiconductor stocks, Micron as a perfect poster child,
that stock peaked in June and has not been able to rally subsequent good earnings
reports.
You had the core weave news, of course, with the spike in their cost of capital, CDS blowing
out for them.
I felt that this is such an enormous contributor to economic growth and the stock market,
and then the stock market tying into economic growth with its influence on upper income
spending that if, and I first said this on Monday before the meeting, that if this trade,
if these concerns in terms of the cost of capital and what that means for the actual build out
of this becomes an economic factor, then the Fed is going to pay attention to it.
Then of course on Wednesday, Kevin Walsh actually said it himself.
He is paying attention.
He sees what's going on.
He said interest rates somehow make their way into every crack when he talked about the
rise in the cost of capital that these companies are experiencing.
I feel like if we fast forward to six weeks from now, the next Fed meeting, if this weakness,
if these concerns continue, now when I say concerns, we know there's going to be a lot
of cap expense this year.
We're talking about the rate of change that matters and whether we're going to see this
same level of construction as is forecast because if you do not, well then you get a ratcheting
back of orders.
You have a negative impact on all the picks and shovels.
You have obviously a response with the stock market, which again ties into consumer spending,
that the Fed has no choice but to make this a factor in determining whether they should
raise rates in December.
This is a very simplistic belief, inflation is still running above target.
It's been so many years.
How can they not hike?
You got to broaden the lens here of what's going on.
I understand.
I'm sympathetic to that.
I'm typically an inflation hawk, but because we're so tethered to this AI trade, you have
no choice but to pay attention and you also have no choice but to start thinking about
what would be the trigger to an eventual unwind because that unwind eventually happens.
It's not a question of if, it's a question of when and is this the beginning of it or
is it not and I think it's going to really be a huge topic of discussion at that next
meeting.
Interesting.
I mean the Fed obviously, we saw that last press conference, I think it was a record 30
minutes.
It lasted right on the dots.
Less seems to be more coming from that guidance.
I mean your note this morning, December, it odds about 84% to 74% to your point big
tech capex, $207 billion in Q3 up from $113 billion.
So I mean what are the odds now by your count for December?
So it's still obviously greater than 50.
That 74% number was in the morning.
I have to see how it's shifted as the day has progressed, but again it's what the
state is of this AI trade and where we are in six weeks because if all of a sudden
there are projects that get cancelled or postponed, there's a big ripple effect.
Everyone talks about the circular financing and that is this like a domino, where right
now we're seeing some ruptures, some cracks underground like here, here, here, but is
it going to be connected in some way and that's what the market is trying to figure
out.
On one hand, you hear from the hyperscalers still talking about very robust capex.
They have yet to give us their 27 estimates and likely it will be higher than 26, but
to what extent?
So that's the bull case.
The bear case is as well, it doesn't matter because maybe the rate of change is slowing
as I said and stuff is not going to get built.
Is there still that Warsh put, a Fed that steps in if stocks fall?
I think Warsh unlike previous Feds is going to be very reluctant, but what does that even
mean when you look at history?
The bear market in the early 2000s and in 2009, the Fed slashed rates all throughout
their bear market.
That didn't stop stocks from falling and the S&P 500 from falling 50% twice.
Now there is this belief, okay, don't worry, the Fed will backstop us now, but okay, well,
they tried those two times, it didn't work.
They obviously then got into QE and OE, but who's to say rate cuts are going to matter?
Now are rate cuts going to save the AI tech trade when spending eventually slows?
No, it's not.
I beg investors not to make their buy and sell decisions based on what they think the
Fed will eventually do to save the day.
That makes sense.
I mean, you were talking about the mainstream numbers before.
Did they surprise you?
Q3 growth was 3.4% PC inflation, 3.6%, I mean, a lot of people would say, how can
the Fed stand down with numbers like that?
Because again, it's all very narrowly focused.
So much is dependent on the AI trade and also a big contributor had about 55 basis points
of the GDP growth was healthcare.
Well, the government is going to continue to via Medicare, Medicaid continue to support
healthcare and the aging population, so there's nothing that monetary policy can
do with that.
Also, what goosed the headline GDP number was a lower than expected inflation deflator
that came in nine-tenths below expectations.
If it was in line, GDP growth would have been 2.5% instead of 3.4%.
So it's important to look under the hood because it's a very narrow contribution
of growth, which is great when it's working, but the market is beginning to sniff out
like what happens if it doesn't.
What do you think?
I mean, I think it was the friendly family fight that they said kind of got, and I
was surprised.
I mean, there was a lot of people that were for, everyone seems like in the committee
they were, other than a couple of dissents, pretty accurate with what Warsh was
saying.
I mean, who on that committee changes their votes because stock chips fall?
We're going to maybe know in the next couple of weeks when they start speaking.
We had one nonvoter today, Alberto Musalem, who is looking at only the inflation
numbers and saying hike.
So we're going to see which of the Fed members really incorporate all this
information that's going on, or those that say, okay, inflation is here, we're
here, we need to act and respond that way.
I think Kevin Warsh, the interesting thing about him is he is very wide with
his head analysis in terms of what he looks at.
Working for Stan Druckenmiller almost forced him to be that way, and he's paying
attention to credit default swaps.
He's paying attention to all these different things, whereas I doubt
Jay Powell was doing that, and you can be sure Ben Bernanke was not paying
attention to credit default swaps in 2008 when he said subprime is contained.
Now, whether his colleagues look at it the same way as he does, well, Musalem
does not, but I think others are going to listen to Warsh when he tells them,
you guys got to start paying attention to this.
There was an argument that people were making because he used the word
superintelligence in the speech, and that made people say, okay, maybe he's
listening to the White House a little bit, maybe this is why we didn't go into
the midterms with a hike.
What are your thoughts on this whole debate?
Well, I take the politics out.
I think that he just raised the AI situation as now something on their
dashboard is people should take that message, and that's why I made my
point that I thought they should pay attention, he confirmed they're paying
attention, and therefore the rest of us need to pay attention, as this now
being a major factor in determining policy.
But I think at the end of the day, and I felt the same way, too, is that
the Fed is now just tweaking policy.
The September hike was not the beginning of another
rate-hiking cycle.
It was a tweak, and even if they do raise rates in December, it's going
to be a tweak.
This is not the beginning of something more.
So if you're selling your gold because, oh, the Fed is going to go on
this big rate-hiking cycle, that's the wrong reason because it's not
going to happen.
Let's transition over to gold.
Obviously, a big audience here, a little anxious today with the spot
price down at one point over $120.
I was looking just now at about $38.90 on the spot side.
Now, you wrote that without a hike, the dollar weekend's real rates
fall, and as you said, gold should end its corrective move.
What happens first?
So fundamentally, things have to shift, and I think they're in the
process.
The two major factors, and I'll add three, for the self and gold
issue, the technical factor was you go straight up, you need a period
of consolidation, and we're now nine months into this consolidation.
The two fundamental factors that were headwinds this year was the
rise in real rates and the strength in the U.S. dollar.
Well, now, real rates are now rolling over because maybe the Fed
doesn't hike again, and now the dollar, I think, is very vulnerable
because not only because on the rate side, but the whole world is
long U.S. tech stocks.
The rally in U.S. tech stocks this year, I think, has been an
underpinning factor to the dollar.
If the trade starts to further sell off from here, if foreigners
say, okay, I need to lighten up on my U.S. stocks position, that's
going to be a weaker dollar, too.
So I do think that the fundamentals are now shifting back in gold's
favor that will eventually create that bottom after this sort of
technical flush out that's taking place.
The last thing that I am very much focused on is next week, I
think it will be next week or maybe the week after, maybe you
know better than I do, the World Gold Council is going to update
their third quarter numbers.
If you do see another quarter of robust central bank buying, I
think from a confidence perspective, that will go a long way
because that would imply that they took advantage of the lower
price to further add to that, to the holding.
So I am looking for hopefully another 200 plus ton quarterly
purchase by central banks as another fundamental underpinning.
The move below 4,000 kind of surprised you a little bit here.
For a lot of people, it did.
You also just talked about it.
The whole world is long, it seems, U.S. tech.
If they sell tech, do they sell gold to cover?
That's what I am thinking over the last couple of weeks, that
the gold has had this very unusual tight correlation with the
I noticed it last week and that tells me that gold is not trading
on its own fundamentals, there is a 4 seller out there, whether
it's margin driven or whatever.
I have a feeling that at least today, this is 4 selling.
This is not on a fundamental thesis at all, which tells me that
this is sort of like the end of this move, just as something
will go up more than you think, sometimes it will go down more
than you think.
I think that we broke this 4,000, which technically has been a
level of support.
Breaking down sort of flushes things out, but anybody that
has a time horizon more than a week, I think this is a pretty
good opportunity.
I mean it's gapped 4,000 all day, so I mean it's sitting
between these ranges.
Let's talk about the cash burn going back to the AI space
because Amazon says it will spend meaningfully more in 2027.
When the biggest companies stop generating cash, I mean who keeps
buying the index?
So that's the bear case, meta, Amazon, Google, Oracle, all now
casually negative.
Microsoft is really the only big hyper-scary left that's still
generating cash flow, but they even argued that they may have
to tap the financing markets.
The bull case is after 2027, 2028, the CapEx cycle starts to
slow and they're going to gush cash flow.
Maybe that's the case.
I think that while those cash flow numbers will certainly
reverse, that they're embedding in their business models a higher
level of expenses, whether it's maintenance CapEx and
continuously having to upgrade these facilities with the new
technology or whether it's persistently higher depreciation
expense as they account for this move.
So I don't think we're going back to the profitability and
margin levels that these companies had prior to the
spend.
So I do think that over time, they're going to be rerated, not
to the levels they were prior to this CapEx blowout.
Now you've seen a little bit of these domino effects before in
the market.
You've been doing this a long time.
I mean, Metaplan is a $95 billion share sale.
Alphabet is raising about $85 billion.
I mean, what happens when the biggest buyers of stock become
sellers?
Yes, this is a big sea change.
This is a change in the market and I think investors have to
incorporate that and to the extent they need to value these
companies, the flood of demand for stock is reversing as you
said.
So Intel, I haven't looked at the stock price intraday, but
it's morning at 30, so it's 20 before market down about 30.
Really huh?
No, it's taxpayers.
Yeah, of course.
Yeah, the country does own a little bit of part of that.
Let's talk about that.
I mean, the Intel CEO says memory prices will be a very
severe issue in 2027.
Is AI pushing up cost for the rest of tech?
Well, Intel specifically is blaming the PC business because of
the higher memory costs.
Consumers are obviously very price sensitive to the price
increases we've seen, which will be interesting to hear what
Apple has to say on that with the price increases they've had
with their phones.
But even Intel with their data center business, which is
obviously their best part of their business, even in their
call last night talked about their difficulties in actually
meeting a lot of that demand from a supply perspective.
But valuations got extended and investors have to understand
that because I'm getting pushback like, yeah, spending
is still going to be up broadly in 2027.
I said yes, but when a company goes from growing 40% to only
growing 30% or maybe growing then 20%, they're still seeing
robust growth.
But that rate of change slowing down has ripple effects not
only for their earnings that they're experiencing, but the
order rates that flow through the supply chain.
So we're going to get higher CapEx spend in 2027 relative to
2026, but stock prices and valuations sniff out that
change and if you don't get as much capacity being built
next year, that means that order books are going to have
to shrink.
Perhaps we're seeing Caterpillar's data center power
sales grew 75% the stock's down about 40% from June.
What's the market telling you there?
It's telling us on the supply side of the data center
construction that maybe we don't get all those gigawatts
of power that were planned for next year.
I think also this is more related to open AI and
anthropic, which is of course at the center of this
whole ecosystem and their profitability will determine the
cloud business for the hyperscalers and all the
obligations that they created on the picks and shovel
side is to what extent is the profitability going to be
negatively impacted by the Chinese competition?
These companies are now in a price war and can
anthropic and open AI make the profitability numbers
that will allow them the cash flow to finance all the
obligations that they committed themselves to in
the coming years.
That's another big question.
I need to know what a day like this looks like for
you.
Are you in your phone, are you buying dips because
more than 400 S&P, 500 companies obviously, the
stocks rose just yesterday.
The NASDAQ fell, is this the rotation you're looking
for?
I am very focused on owning non-AI things right
now.
I think while gold is treated like an AI stock
today, which it's not, it is not and it will recover.
My other favorite sector which is the ultimate X or
non-AI trade are the consumer staple stocks and we
own a bunch of them that happen to be up today.
As market investors look to other things that are
maybe non-AI, investors that are over their
skis on this AI trade, regardless of how great the
technology is, need to position size properly
because it's been such a ride that maybe this
ride is sort of late in the day.
To your point, Wall Street is punishing earnings.
These misses are harder than at any point since
I guess the question is, is that a scared market
or a smart market?
Well, it's probably a combination.
Smart in the sense that they're reassessing the
sustainability and the growth rates of this on
the construction side.
Smart in that they are wondering what's the
ultimate profitability of all this spend in response
to the competition.
But there's also obviously fear involved because
that's just part of Wall Street.
Speak to that fear for a moment because there's
a lot of people watching.
I mean their retirees index fund, it's obviously
heavy in tech as you know, is that still a safe
default at this point?
Well, the interesting thing and the scary thing
and up until this point, the profitable thing
was imagine financial advisor walking into a room
of retirees and said, I have a great idea.
We're going to put half your retirement fund in
one idea, one stock encompassing that idea.
They kick you out of the room.
But that's essentially what this trade has happened
with the S&P 500.
It is one idea.
So to my point earlier, everyone should be reassessing
their exposure and to what extent they want to be
in it because it is very much riding on one idea.
I got to ask you about fewer votes, another
headline that made it.
I mean the Fed still meets eight times a year but
it votes on rates only seven times in 2007 and
six in 2028.
I mean fewer votes, bigger moves?
I don't know.
It's part of Kevin Walsh's desire and I actually
happen to agree with him to let the market voice
more of an opinion and not to be dependent on
what the Fed is saying.
Now, he's been sticking to that.
Of course, his colleagues are not their story
up in a way but I think there's nothing wrong
with that and markets are perfectly capable of
adjusting the level of interest rates based on
where they think the fundamental influences are.
Now, how much of this is political?
I mean without getting political but ahead of
the midterms, is there a little bit of fear?
I mean I think the VIX today obviously taking
a bit of a spike up.
A lot of people are wondering what's happening.
There's uncertainty out there.
I think there's no question that politics
seeps into that room.
They're not going to tell you what does but
they're saying to themselves, okay, why should
I hike a week before the election?
If I want to hike, I can wait another six
weeks, big deal.
So yeah, politics matter and it would be silly
to say it doesn't even though they'll tell
you what doesn't.
Yeah, it makes sense.
We've got to talk about Japan just briefly
here.
I mean Japan Central Bank says inflation
finally matches its 2% target.
What happens to your yields if Japanese
money goes there or goes home?
I think anybody who is trying to figure
out where US rates go, they have no choice
but to focus on what's going on in Japan.
To me, a major macro thing took place in
2023 when the Bank of Japan got rid of
yield curve control.
They were the foot on the neck of
global interest rates through their
repression for many decades and that
removal was sort of the ball lifting up
out of the pool and it could no longer
be suppressed anymore.
So we saw long-term interest rates rise
dramatically in Japan.
Now they're sort of just dragging their
feet again.
They only have their overnight rate
at one and a quarter percent.
They can get control of the long end
if they continuously raise interest
rates but if they drag their feet again
and long-term interest rates in Japan
continue to rise, that will ripple
effect through the Europe and the US
and if Japanese money then comes home
because there are more attractive
opportunities in JGB yields, well,
they own a lot of the European bond
market.
They own a lot of the French bond
market in particular and of course
they're the largest foreign holder
of US Treasuries.
So it very much matters for us
and in Europe what happens in Japanese.
Which one do you watch?
You watch the Japanese bonds or the yen?
Both, 100% both because they're very
much interrelated.
It's interesting because the Bank of
Japan will sell stocks, funds faster
from January, that's what they've
announced here.
I think it was 860 billion yen a year
from 330 billion yen.
Who's the buyer?
Well, they'll just slowly, when I
say slowly, they're going from their
previous timeline of 110 years to sell
their holdings to 43 years and they'll
be buyers, it's just a matter of what
price.
There's always a buyer.
We'll have to see how the market
responds and where investors are
willing to step up.
So it's still being stretched out to
a great extent, just about a third of
the pace previously.
And you brought up France, of course
I'm going to have to talk about it,
France's economy shrank in Q3.
Their borrowing cost hit 5% for the
first time since 2002.
Where does the next bond scare start?
Well, it certainly started in Japan.
I think that accounted for the U.S.
move in yields to 5% in 2023.
Deaths and deficits prove that they
matter.
I know some people argue it doesn't
matter here but French yields are not
rising because growth is robust there.
It's because deaths and deficits
matter there.
And I think those factors are going
to be with us for the next couple
of years.
Deaths and deficits, competition for
capital, still very sticky and
persistent inflation.
This is all going to be an
influence.
Now, we're seeing obviously this
dipping yields.
It started with German bond yields
when the worst day that French
yields spiked, all of a sudden
German bonds became a flight to
safety and within minutes the U.S.
Treasuries did as well.
So we're getting a little rally
here, a little respite, which I
think can continue for a period of
time.
But I still think the trend
longer-term in long-term interest
rates is still higher.
Interesting.
And, you know, the euro just said
it's worst month against the pound
since 2022.
I mean, is the euro the weak
link here?
Well, it's weak because of the
French situation and we'll see
whether that continues.
But, yes, it's interesting that the
U.K. guilt market and the pound
became sort of a beneficiary,
particularly with the new
government and the new budget that
released this week that was, I
guess, benign.
It wasn't dramatic in either way
on the spending or tax side.
But there's still debts and
deficit issues there as well.
And to your point on the
Francis, we've got to see how
it goes.
But, I mean, Q3 down 0.1% debt
near 120% of the GDP gap over
Germany, as you just talked
about, why does since the euro
crisis?
So, I mean, regards leaving in
February, you put this all
together.
I mean, can the ECB actually
hike with France like this?
Well, we'll see.
They leave themselves open to
that.
Of course, when they caught
last time, they talked about
the influence.
They're not going to hike just
because the oil prices are up.
They're looking for the
secondary effects of that.
And if that continues, it's
possible.
But we also have to keep in
mind that the ECB caught their
deposit rate down to 2%.
They were very aggressive.
They went right back to
interest rates.
I'm like, guys, didn't you
learn any lesson from the last
time?
So, even right now, they're at
I think two and a quarter, maybe
it's twice, maybe two and a
half.
They still have rates below the
level of inflation.
So, there's still room for them
to move.
But, yeah, they're going to be
sensitive to the same thing the
Fed is going to be sensitive.
The state has AI trade because
they're going to be directly
impacted if this rolls over as
well.
Yeah, bringing this home back to
us again, there's obviously a
lot of borrowing going on.
Treasury sold a record of
$839 billion a debt in one week.
Most of that is rolled over old
bills, as you know, and U.S. debt
hit 100% of the GDP in the
fiscal year ending on September
30th for the first time since
So, I mean, I think I know the
answer to this, but who's
buying?
Well, there's always going to
be a buyer at a price, and the
question is, what price does
credit get rationed to bring in
those buyers?
Well, you saw with CoreWeave
that that price is 15% on their
unsecured debt.
With U.S. Treasuries, it's less
so foreigners.
You know, the foreign allocation
has obviously shrunk to about
It was 50% 10 years ago.
So it's domestic buyers.
It's banks.
It's pension funds.
It's insurance companies.
It's individuals, because the
government's interest expense is
our interest income for those
that own Treasuries.
And we have to remember, 15
years of zero rates, people
were just dying for income, and
now they actually have it, so
that's who's buying.
But again, it's a matter of what
price they were willing to lend
the U.S. government money.
Now, we're going to air this
before November 4th, so I can
bring it up.
But there's a lot of people
talking about they expect
Treasury to signal a bigger
note in bond sales on
November 4th.
What does that do to the
long-term rates?
I think right now, in the
short term, it's not going to
matter much.
But if I'm right, that's in
deficits matter, among other
factors, then, yeah, it's just
continuing the trend of ever
greater needs for more
financing.
And I'll extend this out.
If the AI tech trade continues
to crack, if the U.S. economy
slows down, that 6% U.S. budget
deficit is going to be 8, it's
going to be 10, and just imagine
how many Treasuries are going
to need to be sold under that
scenario.
Yeah, you know, it was
interesting.
I was reading a report in
Bloomberg this morning.
There was one bond dealer
talking about the number one
risk, and the quote is people
are going to demand higher
yields.
I mean, is he right?
Yeah, I think that's the
case.
But that's generally.
That's for corporate
credit, investment grades,
spreads are widening out.
If you're a triple C company,
it's going to cost you 15%
to borrow money.
So the cost of capital is
going higher for everybody.
Yeah.
So, I mean, if buyers ever
stop, I mean, what does
gold do?
Well, they'll always be those
buyers, but it's so what does
gold do?
I think at the end of the day,
gold is going to obviously be
a beneficiary because, you
know, there'll be a policy
response to this.
Gold is something you're going
to want to own because if
this is a negative impact on
the US dollar, because we
end up suffering the most
because we're all in on the
AI tech trade, you know,
much less so than the rest
of the world outside of
maybe South Korea.
So is that going to be
dollar negative?
Well, that'll be dollar
positive.
So I think gold still is one
of those assets that will
show itself again after this
correction.
Yeah.
Well, certainly, I'm going to
keep watching it today.
We've got a couple more
after this.
Before I let you go, I got
to ask you about the 60-40
because, you know, take a
retired couple.
They got $500,000, 60% in
stocks, 40% in bonds.
Bonds rallied, stocks fell.
I mean, is 60-40 working
again?
Well, the reason why 60-40
worked for so many decades
is because bond holders got
not only the coupon, but they
got capital appreciation as
you saw this 40-year decline
in interest rates.
The reason why 60-40 stopped
working is because bonds
started going up.
They ended up going down
because people have to
understand that when you
own a bond mutual fund, yes,
you're getting some coupon,
but you're essentially betting
on interest rates.
As opposed to owning an
individual bond that you
can, yes, you're going to
have daily fluctuations in
price, but if you hold to
maturity, you're going to get
your money back.
If I buy a five-year treasury
today, I know I'm getting my
money back in five years.
If I buy a mutual fund with,
call it a five-year duration,
I don't know if my
principal is going to come
back in five years.
But on the flip side, people
actually have now income, so
that 40% can be an income
producing asset for the
holders of it.
Don't expect capital
appreciation, but having
income after 15 years of
zero is rather nice.
I was going to say the falling
knives are happening all
around us today, but yet
there's still a lot of value
in the market and other
sectors.
